Five Apple Watch models can measure your blood pressure and issue an alert for potential hypertension issues. However, the device will not provide actual blood pressure readings.

Some smart rings and other fitness devices on the market can achieve this, but require regular calibration with a traditional cuff blood pressure monitor. The upcoming Signal Ring claims to provide full blood pressure measurements without the need for calibration, citing a trial involving several thousand participants to support its claims……

“Silent Killer”

Abnormally high blood pressure (hypertension) and abnormally low blood pressure (hypotension) can both pose significant health risks.

Between the two, hypertension is the more dangerous, often dubbed the “silent killer” because it can cause severe and irreversible damage to the arteries, heart and brain without any obvious symptoms, often only being detected after triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Especially for elderly individuals, regularly measuring blood pressure is a wise practice, and home cuff blood pressure monitors are available on the market for self-measurement. However, the ideal scenario is fully automated monitoring through a fitness device you wear daily.

Apple Watch Blood Pressure Feature

With the launch of watchOS 26, five Apple Watch models can now measure blood pressure:

  • Apple Watch Series 11
  • Apple Watch Series 10
  • Apple Watch Series 9
  • Apple Watch Ultra 3
  • Apple Watch Ultra 2

However, these devices will not provide you with any readings; instead, they issue an alert when signs of potential hypertension are detected. Other devices such as the Oura Ring operate in a similar manner.

Some fitness devices can indeed provide actual blood pressure readings, but require regular calibration with readings from a cuff blood pressure monitor.

Signal Ring

Startup company Vital Signals claims to have successfully developed a smart ring with accuracy comparable to traditional upper-arm cuff blood pressure monitors, and without the need for calibration. This product is the Signal Ring.

According to Bloomberg, company CEO Tom Moss said he nearly lost his life due to undiagnosed hypertension, an experience that spurred him to found the company.

The ring will begin pre-orders later today, ship in October, priced at $399, with no subscription required. Real-time blood pressure readings and long-term tracking data will be displayed through the companion app (see image above).

It is worth noting that the Signal Ring has not yet been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), but clinical trials have shown that the blood pressure readings it obtains are extremely accurate across several thousand participants.

Interestingly, Moss has no intention of selling this ring to the general public — he stated that these professional features are best suited for elderly individuals, and those who have been told by a doctor that they are at risk of hypertension, implying the Signal Ring may not be particularly outstanding in other aspects (such as sleep tracking).
